A loanword is a word that one language permanently takes from another language and begins to use as its own.

Despite the name, there is no "loan" in the real sense — the word is never given back. The name is simply a metaphor: the language "borrows" a word the way you might borrow something from a neighbor, except it never returns it. The word becomes a permanent resident of the new language.
A simple way to picture it

Imagine two groups of people who speak different languages and begin trading with each other. Group A has a food that Group B has never seen before. Group B doesn't have a word for it, so they simply start using Group A's word for it. Over time, that word becomes a completely normal part of Group B's language. That is a loanword.

English is one of the most loanword-heavy languages in the world. Here are some common words that English borrowed — and most people never realize it:

From Italian: pizza, piano, umbrella, balcony
From French: café, ballet, genre, chef, bureau
From German: kindergarten, hamburger, pretzel, angst
From Japanese: karaoke, sushi, emoji, tsunami
From Arabic: sofa, sugar, algebra, alcohol, cotton
From Hindi: shampoo, jungle, bungalow, avatar, thug
From Nahuatl (the Aztec language): chocolate, tomato, avocado, chili
From West African languages: banana, yam, jazz
From Czech: robot

When you say "I had a pizza in my pyjamas while shampooing my hair," you have just used loanwords from Italian, Hindi, and Hindi again — without thinking about it for even a second. That is the hallmark of a true loanword: it has been absorbed so completely that it feels native.
What happens when a word is borrowed

When a language takes in a loanword, one of two things typically happens:

The word may be adopted almost unchanged, keeping its original spelling and sound close to the original. Pizza still sounds and looks Italian. Sushi still looks and sounds Japanese.

Or, the word may be adapted to fit the sounds, spelling rules, or grammar of the new language. The Hindi word chāmpo (which meant "to press or knead the scalp") became the English word shampoo — adjusted to fit how English words sound and how English speakers could say it comfortably.

Either way, once the word settles in and speakers use it naturally without thinking of it as foreign, it is considered a loanword.
A special kind of loanword: the calque

Sometimes, instead of borrowing the word itself, a language translates it piece by piece. This is called a calque (also called a loan translation), and it is considered a type of loanword.

For example, the English word skyscraper was translated into German as Wolkenkratzer, which literally means "cloud-scratcher." The German language didn't borrow the English sounds — it borrowed the idea and built a new word using German pieces. That rebuilt word is a calque.

Similarly, the English phrase flea market came from the French marché aux puces (market of fleas) — English translated the concept rather than copying the French sounds.
The difference between a loanword and a "foreign word"

Not every word from another language automatically becomes a loanword. There is a subtle but important distinction.

A loanword has been fully absorbed into the language. Native speakers use it comfortably, naturally, and usually without even knowing it came from elsewhere. Sofa is a loanword in English — virtually no English speaker thinks of it as Arabic.

A foreign word is one that still feels like a visitor. It is used in the language but still carries a sense of foreignness. For many English speakers, words like schadenfreude (German: pleasure from others' misfortune) or je ne sais quoi (French: a certain something) still feel distinctly foreign — sometimes even written in italics or explained in parentheses to signal that they haven't fully settled in.

The line between the two is not fixed. A word can start as a foreign word and gradually become a loanword as more people use it more naturally over time. Language is always shifting.

No language exists in total isolation. Whenever people from different cultures meet — through trade, war, travel, colonization, technology, or art — languages influence each other. One culture introduces a new concept, object, food, or idea, and the other culture needs a word for it. Taking the original word is often the easiest solution.

This is why loanwords cluster around cultural exchange points. English borrowed heavily from French after the Norman conquest of England in 1066, which is why English has so many French-origin words in law (jury, justice), cooking (cuisine, sauce), and nobility (royal, noble). English borrowed science and mathematics terms from Arabic during the Middle Ages, when Arab scholars led the world in those fields (algorithm, cipher, zenith). And English borrows from technology-leading cultures today, which is why words like emoji and anime are now standard English.

A loanword is a word that one language has permanently taken from another and made its own. It is not a translation — it is the actual word, or a version of it, transplanted into a new language. Loanwords exist in every language because cultures have always been in contact with one another, and language naturally reflects that contact. By the time a loanword is fully settled in, most speakers don't know it ever came from anywhere else — and that invisibility is the clearest sign that the borrowing was a success.
